 Follow Us On: News India Rs 94-lakh Patek Philippe watch seized at IGI. How flyer from Dubai was busted Rs 94-lakh Patek Philippe watch seized at IGI. How flyer from Dubai was busted in Green Channel
 A Rs 94-lakh Patek Philippe Aquanaut watch landed an Indian passenger in trouble at Delhi airport after he was intercepted in the Green Channel. Why did a pre-owned luxury watch trigger a custom alert, and what do India's baggage rules say about carrying expensive watches from abroad?
 Advertisement Delhi Customs held the passenger arriving from Dubai following suspicion and profiling relating to the luxury watch he was carrying. (Image: X/@AirportGenCus and AI-edit) By: India Today News Desk New Delhi , Nov 18, 2026 13:58 IST Last Updated Nov 18, 2026 13:58 IST Published by Avinash Kateel Nov 18, 2026 11:54 IST Written By Avinash Kateel A luxury watch worth nearly Rs 1 crore can catch the eye at an airport. But for an Indian passenger arriving from Dubai, a "pre-owned" Patek Philippe Aquanaut ended up drawing the attention of customs officials instead, triggering a metal detector alert and eventually leading to an arrest.
 The watch, valued at Rs 94 lakh, was seized at Delhi's Indira Gandhi International (IGI) Airport after customs officers intercepted the passenger on the basis of intelligence. The passenger was arrested under the Customs Act, 1962, with officials citing the recovery of the Swiss-made luxury timepiece.
 advertisement ❮ ❯ Read Full Story The seizure has brought the spotlight back on India's customs rules governing expensive personal belongings brought into the country by international travellers. So, what exactly triggered the arrest? Why did the passenger who was meant to pass through the Red Channel, land up in the Green Channel? HOW DELHI CUSTOMS OFFICIALS RECOVERED THE RS 94 LAKH WORTH WATCH
 According to Delhi Customs (Airport and General), officers at Terminal 3 intercepted an Indian passenger arriving from Dubai on November 11 aboard SpiceJet flight SG5106.
 The authority, in a post on X on Tuesday (November 17), said it acted on intelligence, officials diverted the passenger to X-ray screening and a personal and baggage search within the Green Channel. During the examination, the Door Frame Metal Detector (DFMD) triggered an alert.
 The Green Channel and Red Channel are customs clearance paths at international airports that let arriving passengers declare goods or walk through based on what they are carrying.
 A search later led to the recovery of a "pre-owned" Patek Philippe Aquanaut luxury wristwatch. A Chartered Engineer examined the timepiece, certified it as genuine and assessed its value at Rs 94 lakh.
 Customs officials seized the watch under Section 110 of the Customs Act, 1962, and arrested the passenger under Section 104 of the Act. Further investigation is underway.
 In the same post on X, Delhi Customs advised international travellers to declare all dutiable goods and use the Red Channel instead of the Green Channel when required. WHY WAS A PRE-OWNED WATCH SEIZED BY DELHI CUSTOMS?
 The fact that the watch was old and used does not automatically exempt it from customs duty. What matters is whether it qualifies as a duty-free personal effect or falls under the category of imported goods on which customs duty is payable.
 Under India's Baggage Rules, 2026, eligible Indian residents and tourists of Indian origin arriving in India by air are entitled to a general duty-free allowance of Rs 75,000.
 The rules also separately provide for the used personal effects required to meet a traveller's daily necessities during the journey.
 However, the general duty-free allowance is subject to prescribed conditions. It does not mean that every expensive item carried by a passenger automatically qualifies for duty-free entry.
 advertisement Passengers carrying goods that attract customs duty are required to declare them and use the Red Channel for clearance. Those who have no dutiable goods to declare can use the Green Channel.
 In the Delhi case, the watch's valuation of Rs 94 lakh was over 125 times higher than the general duty-free allowance. The customs officials have not publicly disclosed the passenger's declaration, the circumstances in which the watch was being carried or the specific alleged violation that led to its seizure, till the time this report was published.
 Therefore, the valuation alone should not be treated as proof of a customs offence. - Ends (Written by Avinash Kateel)
